description: Georgia's minor tolling statute is a safety net for the child. It is not a safety net for you, a malpractice case, or a notice letter to a city.
shortAnswer: Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90(b), a child generally has until the 20th birthday to file the child’s own claim. Tolling is a safety net for the child. It is not a safety net for you, not a safety net for a malpractice case, and not a safety net for a notice letter to a city.

sections.heading: What the statute actually says
sections.shortAnswer: “Tolling” means the clock is paused. A child hurt in a car wreck, a dog attack, a fall, or a defective-product case generally has until the 20th birthday to file the child’s own claim. The two years start at 18.

sections.heading: Your claim is not your child’s claim
sections.shortAnswer: The parent who has the right to recover for the child’s medical expenses holds that claim, not the child. The parents’ claims for their child’s medical expenses were not tolled by the child’s minority.

sections.heading: Medical malpractice is a different statute, and it is much shorter
sections.shortAnswer: A child who was five or older when the negligence happened is on the adult clock. A child who was under five has two years from the fifth birthday. Behind both of those sits a statute of repose.

sections.heading: Notice deadlines are not the lawsuit deadline
sections.shortAnswer: If a city is the defendant, O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5 requires an ante litem notice within six months, and the minor tolling statute does not apply to that notice. Miss the six months and the claim is gone.

sections.heading: A few other walls the tolling statute does not move
sections.shortAnswer: A product claim can run into the ten-year statute of repose in O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11. If you are the parent suing for the death of your child, that claim is yours. Your child’s age does not pause it.

sections.heading: What I tell parents to do
sections.shortAnswer: Do not treat tolling as permission to wait. If a city, a county, or the State may be involved, send the notice now.

faq.q: Is a parent's claim for a child's medical bills tolled until the child turns 18 in Georgia?
faq.a: No. The parent who has the right to recover for the child’s medical expenses holds that claim, not the child. In Swallows v. Adams-Pickett, 344 Ga. App. 647 (2018), the parents’ claims for their child’s medical expenses were not tolled by the child’s minority. File both, or at least protect both, inside the ordinary two years.

faq.q: How long does a child have to file a medical malpractice claim in Georgia?
faq.a: A child who was five or older when the negligence happened is on the adult clock: two years from the injury, under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71. A child who was under five has two years from the fifth birthday. If the child was under five at the time of the act, the suit may not be brought after the tenth birthday.

faq.q: Does a child get until 18 to send the six-month ante litem notice to a Georgia city?
faq.a: No. In Dates v. City of Atlanta (Ga. June 10, 2025), the Supreme Court of Georgia held that the minor tolling statute does not apply to that notice. A child hurt on city property does not get until age 18 to send the letter. Miss the six months and the claim is gone.

faq.q: When does a child's injury settlement need court approval in Georgia?
faq.a: If the offer to settle is more than $25,000, O.C.G.A. § 29-3-3 requires court approval before that settlement binds your child. A gross settlement of $25,000 or less can be compromised by the natural guardian without court approval and without a conservator.
